04 · Read & review

The transcript

Submit all six answers to unlock the transcript. You can then listen and read together.

James had granted Emma five minutes, a narrow concession she had no right to mistake for forgiveness. Already in the kitchen, he introduced his mother, Nora, and remained nearby. She stood at the window, watching rain collect along the lower edge of the glass. Beyond it, the garden looked as though it had been allowed to grow on its own terms. Emma resisted the urge to interrupt. Years of reporting had taught her that a silence, properly left alone, could reveal more than a question asked too soon.

“When Claire went missing,” Nora said, “people were desperate for the event to mean something recognisable. A quarrel. An accident. A stranger. Anything that could be fitted into a story and put away.”

“And you saw something that didn't fit?”

“I saw something I didn't know how to interpret. There's a difference.”

Emma placed her notebook on the table, still closed.

“I told the police I'd seen Claire that evening. I've repeated that much to myself for fifteen years. It was true, as far as it went.” Nora turned from the window. “But I kept coming back to the part I hadn't explained properly.”

“Tell me only what you're sure you remember,” Emma said.

Nora sat opposite her. She folded a tea towel into a narrow rectangle and straightened its edges before speaking again.

“I was walking home. The light was going, but it wasn't dark. There was a car near the turning, stopped off the road. Claire stood beside it. She was carrying a bag. I recognised her straight away.”

“Did she notice you?”

“Not that I could tell. I almost called out. Then I thought perhaps I'd only be intruding.”

“What happened?”

“She opened the passenger door and got in. There was no struggle that I saw, no one holding her by the arm. The car pulled away before I'd made up my mind to speak.”

Emma felt an immediate temptation to arrange these details into an explanation. She recognised the temptation for what it was: the same impatience that had once allowed an insufficiently checked account to become a newspaper story.

“Did Claire appear to be leaving of her own accord?” she asked, then corrected herself. “No. That's unfairly put. What could you actually see?”

Nora gave a brief, tired smile. “That's the question I've been asking myself all these years. I could see her open a door. I couldn't see whether she was frightened. I couldn't see what had been said before I arrived. And I certainly couldn't see the choices she believed were available to her.”

Emma wrote the answer down almost word for word.

“Why didn't the account emerge clearly at the time?”

“I can't tell you precisely what I said in that interview. I remember telling the police I'd seen her. I remember answering questions. But if I claim I can reproduce the conversation after fifteen years, I'm doing exactly what I don't want you to do: making a memory sound more complete than it is.”

Emma underlined not a verbatim recollection. The distinction mattered. Nora's present account could provide a lead without establishing what had been recorded in 2011. Both the original statement and the new recollection would need scrutiny.

“For a long time,” Nora continued, “I thought the fact that she got in herself settled the question. Then I began wondering what 'herself' meant. People can take an action without making a free decision. Fear doesn't always look like resistance.”

“And that uncertainty kept you silent?”

“Partly. I was frightened of becoming another person who claimed to know Claire's mind. People spoke about her as if she were either helpless or selfish. I knew neither of those things.”

Emma watched Nora flatten the tea towel again. Silence had not preserved the truth intact; it had merely allowed other explanations to grow around the gap.

“If you write about this,” Nora said, “promise me you won't say she left happily. Or even willingly, without explaining what that word can and cannot establish.”

“I'll describe the action you witnessed,” Emma replied. “I won't pretend it tells us her reasons.”

Outside, the rain had eased. Emma had arrived hoping for a definitive answer and was leaving with something less comfortable: an observation that could change the investigation, provided she did not ask it to prove more than it could.
